list.listitem: Suspect secondary bacterial peritonitis in a patient with an ascitic fluid infection and a surgically treatable intra-abdominal source. C

Ascitic fluid analysis can be used to help diagnose secondary bacterial peritonitis, and acute abdominal series radiographs (supine and erect abdominal views, erect chest), CT abdomen, and abdominal ultrasound can help identify the source of intra-abdominal infection. C
Treatment requires prompt source control via surgical intervention and/or peritoneal drainage in addition to antibiotics. C
The mortality of secondary bacterial peritonitis approaches 100 percent if surgical intervention is delayed. B

For empiric therapy of community-acquired, intra-abdominal (CA-IAI) infection in lower risk patients, the Surgical Infection Society (SIS) guidelines recommend narrower spectrum antimicrobial agents such as (1) cefotaxime or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole, (2) ertapenem, or (3) ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole or moxifloxacin monotherapy in patients with serious β-lactam allergies.A
For empiric therapy of CA-IAI in higher risk patients, SIS guidelines recommend against aminoglycoside-based combination regimens.A

SIS guidelines recommend limiting antimicrobial therapy to no more than four days after adequate source control and to 24 hours for patients with traumatic bowel perforations operated on within 12 hours, acute or gangrenous appendicitis without perforation, or acute or gangrenous cholecystitis without perforation.A

In higher risk patients at risk of complications from diabetes mellitus, obesity, or higher illness severity, SIS guidelines recommend limiting antimicrobial agent therapy to four days after achieving source control.B

background.definition: Secondary peritonitis refers to peritoneal inflammation due to another condition, generally a pathological process in a visceral organ. It can be further classified into two forms: with and without free perforation of an abdominal viscus.

list.listitem: Secondary peritonitis most often occurs in patients in their 20's (32%) or 30's (26%).
Males are predominantly affected, with a male to female ratio of 9:1.
Secondary peritonitis has been shown to have a global 30-day mortality rate of 25%.
The highest mortality occurrs in patients admitted to the hospital more than 24 hours after symptom onset.
Secondary peritonitis occurs when enteric microorganisms enter the normally sterile peritoneal cavity via a defect in the wall of the intestine or other viscous.
Peptic ulcer perforation is the most common cause (64%), followed by small bowel perforations (24%) and perforated appendicitis (12%).
Other causes include diverticulitis, bowel strangulation, direct trauma, volvulus, malignancy, and bowel infarction.
Anaerobic bacteria enter the peritoneal cavity through an intestinal or other hollow viscus defect from obstruction, infarction, or direct trauma.
The inoculum is spontaneously reduced to include only a few enteric organisms that survive well outside their natural environment, and these are therefore generally mixed infections.

The most common gram negatives are Escherichia coli and to a much lesser extent other Enterobacteriaceae such as Klebsiella spp. or non-fermenting gram-negative aerobes such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Strepptococci, primarily of the Streptococcus milleri group, are also frequently isolated, and much less frequently enterococci in patients with community-acquired infections. Anaerobes like Bacteroides spp. and Bacteroides fragilis are also common, although most of the enteric anerobes involved in these infections are not isolated by clinical laboratories.
Secondary peritonitis occurs in a biphasic pattern where endotoxin-generating facultative anaerobes and obligate anaerobes act in synergy.
Escherichia coli is responsible for the acute peritonitis phase whereas Bacteroides fragilis has been shown to be responsible for late abscess formation.
Microorganisms and their products, such as endotoxins, stimulate the host's immune system to activate a myriad of inflammatory mediators responsible for peritonitis and potentially ensuing sepsis.
Suspect secondary peritonitis in patients with fever, diffuse abdominal pain and rigidity, nausea or vomiting, and rebound tenderness or other peritoneal signs. C

Runyon's criteria for diagnosis of secondary bacterial peritonitis include at least two of the following on ascitic fluid analysis: total protein >1 g/dL, glucose <50 mg/dL, and lactate dehydrogenase greater than the upper limit of normal for serum. C

While imaging is often done as part of the evaluation of the patient with an acute abdomen, it is not needed prior to surgery in patients with obvious signs and symptoms of diffuse peritonitis in whom surgery is planned. Contrast-enhanced CT imaging is the best study to investigate treatment failure, although the need for re-intervention should not be determined solely by CT scanning. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Patients with known liver disease, abdominal rigidity, ascitic fluid with high carcinoembryonic angiten (CEA) or alkaline phosphatase (AP) levels
Often no fever with a predominance of non-PMNs in ascitic fluid
Often no fever with a predominance of non-PMNs in ascitic fluid
Generally associated with nausea, vomiting and/ or diarrhea

list.listitem: Suspect secondary peritonitis in patients with fever (>38°C), diffuse abdominal pain and rigidity, nausea and vomiting.

Signs of peritoneal inflammation include rebound tenderness, abdominal wall rigidity (involuntary guarding), hypoactive bowel sounds, and generalized tenderness elicitable by percussion or light palpation.
Later signs will include sepsis (systemic inflammatory response syndrom [SIRS] + intra-abdominal source of infection), septic shock, and multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS).

Clinical signs are absent in 30% of patients with ascitic fluid infection, as ascites can prevent the development of a surgical abdomen by separating the visceral from the parietal peritoneal surfaces.

Physical exam findings are also typically minimal or absent in patients with early acute mesenteric ischemia whose abdominal pain is initially out of proprotion to their exam findings. Peritonitis and septicemia develop once the ischemia and necrosis have progressed transmurally. Early recognition and intervention are crucial in this rare condition with high mortality, and patients with a history of atrial fibrillation, heart valve disease, or atheroslcerosis should be considered as possibly presenting with acute superior mesenteric artery embolism, the main cause of acute mesenteric ischemia.
See chapter on diagnosis of abdominal pain for more on the general evaluation of patients with abdominal pain.

Initial evaluation in the patient with suspected peritonitis should include ascitic fluid analysis (total protein, glucose, lactate dehydrogenase), acute abdominal series radiographs (supine and erect abdominal views, erect chest), and water-soluble bowel contrast studies.

Peritoneal fluid cultures are not routinely recommended in lower-risk patients for the purpose of guiding antimicrobial therapy; however, obtain peritoneal fluid/infected tissue cultures in higher-risk patients to identify potential resistant or opportunistic pathogens.

Typical laboratory findings include elevated blood leukocyte count with a polymorphonuclear predominance and a decreased ascitic fluid pH. Rising ascitic fluid PMN count or persistently positive ascitic fluid cultures despite 48 hours of treatment helps identify patients with secondary peritonitis. Elevated ascitic fluid carcinoembryonic antigen or alkaline phosphatase suggests spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

Patients with an acute abdomen often have imaging as part of their initial evaluation; however, the need for imaging and the preferred modality depends on the differential diagnosis based on history, physical, and laboratory studies. Imaging is not needed prior to surgery in patients with obvious signs and symptoms of diffuse peritonitis in whom surgery is planned.

Abdominal X-rays may reveal free air due to viscous perforation, dilated small bowel loops with air fluid levels from ileus or obstruction, and obliteration of the psoas muscle shadow indicating adjacent inflammation. If acute mesenteric ischemia is suspected, CTA has superceded angiography as the imaging study of choice given its universal availability and diagnostic accuracy.
CT scan with contrast is the best study to investigate treatment failure, although the need for re-intervention should not be determined solely by CT scanning.

The presence of either obligate anaerobes or a mixed flora in the peritoneal cavity suggests secondary peritonitis; anaerobic bacteria predominate in intra-abdominal infections where they outnumber the aerobic and facultative bacteria by a ratio of 1,000 to 10,000 to 1.

Secondary peritonitis associated with perforation may be identifiable on the basis of the initial ascitic fluid analysis being neutrocytic (PMN count ≥250 cells/mm3) and is characterized by at least two of the following (Runyon's Criteria): ascitic fluid total protein >1 g/dl, glucose <50 mg/dl, or lactate dehydrogenase greater than the upper limit of normal for serum. These criteria are 97% sensitive but only 45% specific for detecting secondary peritonitis associated with perforation. Thus, they are more useful at ruling out secondary peritonitis when absent (i.e. only 0 or 1 criteria present) than at ruling in.
The Mannheim Peritonitis Index can be used to determine the prognosis of patients with peritonitis and has been validated in a study of 2003 patients.
Suspect secondary peritonitis in patients with fever, diffuse abdominal pain and rigidity, nausea or vomiting, and rebound tenderness or other peritoneal signs.

Initial diagnostic testing should include ascitic fluid analysis for total protein, glucose, LDH, pH, and cell counts. Also consider acute abdominal series radioraphs (supine and erect abdominal views, erect chest).

The need for imaging and the modality depends on the differential diagnosis following a history, physical, and labs. Imaging is not needed when obvious signs and symptoms of diffuse peritonitis necessitate emergency surgery. CT scan with contrast is the best study to evaluate initial treatment failure, although the need for re-intervention should not be based solely on CT.

Stabilization of the patient includes correcting fluid and electrolyte deficiencies with parenteral fluids, alleviation of intestinal obstruction with nasogastric suctioning, and controlling infection with antibiotics. C
Prompt surgical intervention is required to stop delivery of bacteria and adjuvants into the peritoneal cavity. C

SIS guidelines recommend cefotaxime or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole or ertapenem (or ciprofloxacine plus metronidazole or moxifloxacin monotherapy when a serious beta-lactam allergy) for lower-risk patients with CA-IAI.A
For empiric therapy of CA-IAI in higher risk patients, SIS guidelines recommend against aminoglycoside-based combination regimens.A

SIS guidelines recommend limiting antimicrobial therapy to no more than four days (96 h) after adequate source control and to 24 hours for patients with traumatic bowel perforations operated on within 12 hours, acute or gangrenous appendicitis without perforation, or acute or gangrenous cholecystitis without perforation.A

In higher risk patients at risk of complications from diabetes mellitus, obesity, or higher illness severity, SIS guidelines recommend limiting antimicrobial agent therapy to four days after achieving source control.B
Decisions regarding empiric therapy should consider local epidemiology. See for recommended regimens in different clinical scenarios based on 2024 SIS guidelines.

A randomized trial of 518 patients with complicated intra-abdominal infection who underwent source control compared 4 days of antibiotics with antibiotics continued for 2 days after symptom resolution (mean 8 days), and there was no difference in outcomes.

A trial randomized 249 patients with postoperative intra-abdominal infection to 8 or 15 days of antibiotic, and there was no difference in 45 day mortality (RD 0.038, 95% CI -0.013 to 0.061), ICU or hospital length of stay, or reoperation rates.
In patients at higher risk patients, SIS guidelines suggest empiric therapy targeting Enterococcus spp.B
SIS guidelines recommend anidulafungin for empiric therapy of higher risk patients with infections from Candida spp.B
A randomized trial of 541 patients with peritonitis found that eravacycline 1 mg/kg q12 hours was non-inferior to ertapenem 1 gm once daily.
Patient outcomes are significantly affected by early surigical intervention and/or peritoneal drainage.

Re-laparotomy with intra-abdominal lavage can control the infectious source and is therefore the recommended operative procedure in most cases of intra-abdominal infection. Re-laparoscopy is an alternative option in hemodynamically stable patients.
A multicenter RCT found better outcomes with "on demand" re-laparotomy (ie, only if symptoms worsened) compared with a scheduled re-laparoscopy for all patients.

In patients with perforated diverticulitis (Hinchey Grade III), several multicenter RCTs showed laparascopic lavage to have a similar mortality to Hartman's procedure (proctosigmoidectomy, anorectal stump, end colostomy) but a higher rate of secondary events such as deep surgical site infections and unplanned reoperations. Furthermore, one of these RCTs needed to be stopped due to an increased event rate and safety concerns in the lavage group.

Interestingly, an RCT of patients with perforated diverticulitis demonstrated some improved outcomes in the lavage group compared to the surgical resection group, with a lower risk of one or more surgeries within 24 months (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.36 - 0.84) and fewer operations (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.31 - 0.87), although there was still no difference in mortality.

Recurrence of diverticulitis is high following successful laparoscopic peritoneal lavage in Hinchey III peritonitis, decreasing after the first year. The risk of new diverticulitis episodes is independently increased by smoking and previous episodes of acute diverticulitis.
Active smoking status and corticosteroid use were risk factors for laparoscopic lavage treatment failure in patients with perforated diverticulitis.

A meta-analysis of RCTs on long-term outcomes of surgical treatment of perforated diverticulitis showed that in Hinchey class III peritonitis (purulent), laparoscopic lavage had lower odds of long-term ostomy and reoperation but more risk for disease recurrence compared to resection. Colonic resection with primary anastomosis had better long-term outcomes than the Hartmann procedure for Hinchey class IV peritonitis (fecal).

In a prospective, randomized clinical trial of patients undergoing emergent laparotomy for secondary peritonitis due to a perforated viscous and bowel ischemia requiring resection, using triclosan-coated sutures and barbed sutures decreased incisional surgical-site infections and evisceration, respectively.

In patients with presumed uncomplicated acute appendicitis, scheduling appendicectomy within 24 h does not increase the risk of appendiceal perforation compared to scheduling within 8 h. These results can help guide operating room resource allocation, such as postponing a late night appendicectomy until the morning.
Stabilization of the patient requires correcting fluid and electrolyte imbalances with parenteral fluids and alleviating intestinal obstruction with nasogastric suctioning.

A meta-analysis identified 4 RCTs with 288 patients comparing albumin infusion with no infusion or artificial colloid and found that albumin infusion reduced both mortality (OR 0.34; 95% CI 0.19-0.60) and renal impairment (OR 0.21; 95% CI 0.11-42).

Complications of peritonitis include septic shock, respiratory failure, retroperitoneal or intra-abdominal abscesses, small-bowel obstruction from adhesions, fistula, and postsurgical wound infection.
Secondary peritonitis has been shown to have a global 30-day mortality rate of 25%. B
For adults with complicated intra-abdominal infection, the APACHE II is the preferred severity of illness score for risk stratification within 24 hours of hospitalization or ICU admission.B
Other peritonitis specific scoring systems include the Mannheim Peritonitis index (MPI) and the Peritonitis Index of Altona II (PIA II).

Among patients with peritonitis secondary to duodenal ulcer, worse prognosis was seen with multiple gut perforations, larger perforations, larger amount of peritoneal fluid, and development of other complications.

A systematic review identified increasing age, concomitant disease, upper GI source, generalized peritonitis, and abnormal bilirubin, creatinine, lactate, and albumin as the most commonly identified variables predicting ongoing infection in patients with secondary peritonitis.

In retrospective cohort of nontrauma patients with peritonitis, early mortality (≤72 hours after emergency laparotomy) was associated with decreased pH, elevated creatinine, and elevated lactate. The CELIOtomy score combines these factors with patient age and Glasgow Coma Scale to create a risk nomogram that is easier to use than the APACHE II score and can help the patient and family make an informed decision when surgical interventions would be futile.

All available tools should be used to share prognostic information with the patient, the family, or their guardians to guide treatment decisions. Vigilance is particularly important in patients with a mortality risk greater than 75% according to ACS NSQIP Surgical Risk Calculator to avoid futility and due consequences.
